title: Longest Common Prefix
description: Brute force to optimized: comparing every pair of strings versus shrinking a running prefix candidate.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of strings strs, find the longest string that is a prefix of every string in the array. If no common prefix exists at all, return an empty string.

blocks.text: Given an array of strings strs, find the longest string that is a prefix of every string in the array. If no common prefix exists at all, return an empty string.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Shared Beginning of a Family's Names
blocks.text: Like noticing that everyone in one family has names starting with the same first few letters. The common prefix is exactly how far that shared beginning extends before the names start to differ.

blocks.caption: Find the longest starting sequence of characters shared by every string

blocks.text: With only one string in the array, the entire string is trivially its own common prefix, so the answer is "single" itself.
It helps to ask whether every one of the n times n minus 1 pairwise comparisons the brute force performs is actually necessary.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force correctly finds the shared prefix length by comparing every pair of strings directly, but this repeats an enormous amount of redundant character-by-character comparison work.

Observation 2: Whatever the final answer is, it must in particular be a prefix of the very first string in the array, since it has to be a prefix of every string, including that one.

Observation 3: That means the first string alone can serve as a starting candidate, and every other string only ever needs to be compared against that single running candidate, never against each other directly, shrinking the candidate whenever it fails to match.

Observation 4: Tracing strs equal to ["flower", "flow", "flight"] confirms it, the candidate shrinks monotonically from "flower" to "flow" to "fl" as each new string is checked, converging on the true longest shared prefix in a single linear pass.
Recognizing that the first string alone can act as a running candidate, checked once against every other string, is what replaces an all pairs comparison with a single linear pass.
Compare every pair of strings directly, letter by letter, to find their shared prefix, and combine the results across every pair.

items: For every pair of strings in the array, compare them character by character to find how far they agree.
Track the shortest such shared prefix length found across every pair.
Return the prefix of that shortest length.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every ordered pair of distinct strings is compared, so no pairwise relationship in the array is missed.
The shortest matching length found across all pairs is kept, since the true common prefix cannot be any longer than the shortest pairwise agreement found anywhere.
The final prefix is sliced directly from the first string, using that shortest matching length as the cutoff.

blocks.text: Every pair of strings is compared directly, so the true shared prefix length across the whole array is correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared times m), comparing every pair of the n strings up to m characters each.
Space: O(1) extra, not counting the output.

Limitation: comparing every pair independently repeats a huge amount of redundant work. A prefix candidate can instead be maintained incrementally and simply narrowed down as each string is checked against it, one at a time.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it treats every pair of strings as if it needed independent verification, when the correct answer is fully determined just by how far every OTHER string agrees with the first one.

What a running candidate fixes directly: starting the candidate as the entire first string and comparing every remaining string only against that single candidate removes the need for any pairwise comparison between two other strings.

What happens when a string does not match the current candidate: the candidate is shrunk from its end, one character at a time, until it does match, since the true answer can never be longer than what every string checked so far agrees on.

The core idea: one running candidate, narrowed by each string in a single left to right pass over the array, replaces an all pairs comparison entirely.

Start with the first string as the current best guess at the common prefix. Then, for every remaining string, shrink that guess from the end until it actually is a prefix of the current string. By the time every string has been checked once, whatever remains is guaranteed to be the true longest common prefix.
Maintain a running prefix candidate, shrinking it against each string in a single pass through the array.

blocks.caption: Optimized: shrink a running prefix candidate against each string in turn

blocks.text: This works because the candidate only ever shrinks, never grows, so once every string in the array has been checked against it, the surviving candidate is by construction a prefix of every single string, and it cannot be any longer, since shrinking only ever happens when a genuine mismatch is found.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The current string already starts with the running candidate","No shrinking is needed, the candidate stays the same","The candidate remains valid for every string checked so far"],["The current string does not start with the running candidate","The candidate is shrunk one character at a time until it matches, or becomes empty","The candidate correctly narrows to the true shared prefix, or proves no common prefix exists"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times m), where every string is compared against the shrinking prefix candidate at most once per character.
Space: O(1) extra, not counting the output.

blocks.text: This is the standard "narrow a running candidate" pattern, which turns an all pairs comparison into a single linear pass, and the same shrinking idea works whether scanning strings horizontally like this or column by column across all strings at once.

Not checking for the prefix candidate shrinking all the way to empty, which should stop early and return immediately rather than continuing to compare an empty string.

blocks.text: Mention the alternative of scanning column by column across all strings at once (checking whether every string shares the same character at position 0, then position 1, and so on) as an equally valid approach with the same time complexity, useful when strings might be very long but share only a short prefix.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid comparing every pair", think: a single running candidate, shrunk against each string in turn.
If the interviewer says "what if the strings are very long but share only a short prefix", think: scan column by column instead, stopping at the first mismatched column across all strings.
If the interviewer says "what if the array is empty", think: return an empty string immediately, there is no string to anchor a candidate on.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared times m) time, O(1) extra space. Optimized: O(n times m) time, O(1) extra space.

items: Pattern: a running prefix candidate, shrunk against each string in turn instead of comparing every pair directly.

Core Idea: any valid common prefix must in particular be a prefix of the first string, so starting there and shrinking the candidate against every remaining string replaces an all pairs comparison with a single linear pass.
Time: O(n squared times m) for the brute force, O(n times m) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) extra for both approaches.
Most Important Observation: the answer is fully determined by comparing every string to just one reference point, the first string, never to each other.
Interview Difficulty: the running candidate idea is simple and standard; mentioning the column by column alternative and when it is preferable is what shows extra awareness.
One line memory trick: start with the first string, shrink it against every other string until it fits.
